question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Between a rock and a hard place
option_1: Stuck between two very bad options
option_4: Avoiding the main topic, not speaking directly about the issue
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Stuck between two very bad options.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom “between a rock and a hard place” means being in a dilemma where both available choices are equally unpleasant. (दो मुसीबतों के बीच फंसना)

◦ It is the English equivalent of “between the devil and the deep blue sea”.

◦ Correct: With no money and no job, he was stuck between a rock and a hard place.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 “Willing to do anything” matches “go to any length”, not this idiom.

• Option 3 “On the point of achievement” matches “on the verge of”.

• Option 4 “Avoiding the main topic” is the meaning of “beat about the bush”.

NOTE

• Similar dilemma idioms: in a fix, in a tight corner, on the horns of a dilemma, caught in a cleft stick.

• SSC repeats: “Hobson’s choice” = no real choice at all (take it or leave it).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘no substitution required’.

The only course of action to (fend of the loud clamour off conspiracy theories) is to keep everyone fully informed.
option_1: fend off the loud clamour of conspiracy theories
option_3: fend off the loud clamour off conspiracy theories
option_4: fend of the loud clamour of conspiracy theories
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. fend off the loud clamour of conspiracy theories.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• “Fend off” is a phrasal verb meaning to ward off / keep away / resist something unpleasant. (बचाव करना)

◦ The noun “clamour” (loud noise/outcry) is followed by the preposition “of” to show what the outcry consists of: *clamour of protest, clamour of voices*.

◦ The printed segment wrongly writes “fend of” and “clamour off” — both prepositions are swapped.

◦ Correct: The only course of action to fend off the loud clamour of conspiracy theories is to keep everyone fully informed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is wrong because the bracketed part is clearly erroneous.

• Option 3 corrects “fend off” but keeps the wrong “clamour off”.

• Option 4 corrects “clamour of” but keeps the wrong “fend of”.

NOTE

• off = away from (adverb/preposition of separation); of = belonging to / consisting of.

• Related phrasal verbs: ward off, stave off, head off, fight off — all mean to keep something away.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

To bear the brunt of
option_3: To endure the impact of something
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To endure the impact of something.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• “To bear the brunt of” means to suffer or endure the main force/worst part of something unpleasant. (सबसे ज्यादा मार झेलना)

◦ “Brunt” itself means the chief impact or shock of an attack.

◦ Correct: Coastal villages bore the brunt of the cyclone.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 “An inexperienced person” is the meaning of a greenhorn / a raw hand.

• Option 2 “For one’s sake” is a prepositional phrase, not this idiom.

• Option 4 “To become free from” matches to get rid of.

NOTE

• Related idioms: face the music = accept unpleasant consequences; weather the storm = survive a difficult period; take the rap = be blamed/punished for another’s fault.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.

You can find these books into the extreme corner of this shelf.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. books into the extreme.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• “Into” shows movement from outside to inside; “in” shows a static position/location. (स्थिति बनाम गति)

◦ The books are simply lying at a place — no motion is involved — so the preposition must be in, not “into”.

◦ Correct: You can find these books in the extreme corner of this shelf.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 “corner of this shelf” is correct — “of” rightly shows possession/part.

• Option 3 “You can find these” is correct — modal “can” + bare infinitive “find”.

• Option 4 is wrong because the sentence does contain an error.

NOTE

• Compare: “He walked into the room” (motion) vs “He is in the room” (position).

• Similar pairs: on/onto, to/till, among/between.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Enzymes can _______ starches into sugars and proteins into amino acids.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. convert.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Convert (verb) = to change something into another form or substance. (बदलना / रूपांतरित करना)

◦ It collocates perfectly with the structure “convert X into Y”, which the sentence already contains.

◦ Correct: Enzymes can convert starches into sugars and proteins into amino acids.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Cover = to place something over/on top of; it does not take “into”.

• Covert = secret, hidden (adjective) — the opposite of “overt”; it is not a verb here.

• Conserve = to protect or save from loss/waste, e.g. conserve water, conserve energy.

NOTE

• Confusable pair: covert (गुप्त) vs convert (बदलना); also overt = open, undisguised.

• Useful collocations: *transform into*, *change into*, *turn into*, *translate into*.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.

Mothers can pass the HIV virus to their newborns during delivery as well, WHO says.
option_2: Mothers can pass the HIV virus to
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. as well, WHO says.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Names of organisations that are read letter by letter take the definite article “the” — *the WHO, the UNO, the CBI, the BBC*. (निश्चित उपपद का प्रयोग)

◦ The segment therefore needs “the WHO says”, not the bare “WHO says”.

◦ Correct: Mothers can pass the HIV virus to their newborns during delivery as well, the WHO says.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is correct — modal “can” + base verb “pass”, and “pass something to somebody” is the right preposition.

• Option 4 is correct — “during delivery” rightly shows a period of time.

• Option 3 is wrong because the sentence does contain an error.

NOTE

• “The” is used with abbreviations pronounced as letters (the FBI), but NOT with acronyms pronounced as words (NASA, UNESCO, UNICEF).

• “The” is also used with rivers, oceans, mountain ranges, newspapers and holy books.

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

And how amorous you become / when your courtship with the / muses is going stronger.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. muses is going stronger.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed collocation for something becoming more intense is “grow stronger”, not “go stronger”. (मजबूत होना)

◦ Grow here is a link verb meaning “become gradually” and is followed by an adjective: *grow older, grow darker, grow stronger*.

◦ Correct: And how amorous you become when your courtship with the muses is growing stronger.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 4 “And how amorous you become” is correct — an exclamatory structure with the adjective “amorous” (loving).

• Option 2 “when your courtship with the” is correct — “courtship with” is the right preposition.

• Option 1 is wrong because the sentence does contain an error.

NOTE

• Link verbs followed by adjectives: grow, become, turn, seem, appear, feel, look, remain, get.

• “Go” + adjective is used only for a change to a bad state: *go bad, go blind, go mad, go sour*.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.

One who is 100 years old or older
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Centenarian.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A centenarian is a person who has lived to or beyond the age of 100 years. (शतायु व्यक्ति)

◦ It comes from Latin *centum* = hundred, the same root as *century* and *cent*.

◦ Correct: The centenarian cut a cake with a hundred candles on it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Immortal = one who never dies / lives forever.

• Mortal = a being who must die; subject to death.

• Sententia is not a standard English one-word substitution; it is a Latin term for a maxim or opinion.

NOTE

• Age-related one-word substitutions: octogenarian (80–89), nonagenarian (90–99), centenarian (100+), supercentenarian (110+).

• Also asked: sexagenarian (60–69), septuagenarian (70–79).

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

The royal messengers ______ out last night.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. went.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The adverbial “last night” is a definite past time marker, so the verb must be in the simple past tense. (सामान्य भूतकाल)

◦ The past form of “go” is went (go – went – gone).

◦ Correct: The royal messengers went out last night.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 “goes” is singular present — it disagrees with the plural subject “messengers” and with the past time.

• Option 2 “go” is present tense and cannot be used with “last night”.

• Option 3 “gone” is the past participle (V3) and needs an auxiliary such as *have/had*.

NOTE

• Simple past markers: yesterday, last night/week/year, ago, in 1995, then, once.

• Present perfect markers (never with “last night”): just, already, yet, since, for, so far, recently.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

He ______ his teeth against the curse on his tongue.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. clenched.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Clench = to press or squeeze tightly together, especially the teeth or the fist, usually out of anger or effort. (कसकर भींचना)

◦ “Clench one’s teeth” is a fixed collocation showing that a person is holding back words or emotion — exactly the sense of holding back “the curse on his tongue”.

◦ Correct: He clenched his teeth against the curse on his tongue.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Dropped = let fall; “dropped his teeth” makes no sense in the context.

• Unclasped = opened or loosened a grip — the exact opposite of what is needed.

• Yielded = surrendered or produced; it does not collocate with “teeth”.

NOTE

• Body collocations: clench the fist/jaw/teeth, grit the teeth, purse the lips, shrug the shoulders, raise an eyebrow.

• “Grit one’s teeth” also means to show determination in the face of difficulty.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Pleasurre.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is “Pleasure” — with a single “r” before the final “e”. (आनंद / खुशी)

◦ “Pleasurre” wrongly doubles the letter r.

◦ Correct: It gives me great pleasure to welcome you all.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Slogan — correctly spelt; a short catchy phrase used in advertising or protest.

• Heaven — correctly spelt; the abode of God, paradise.

• Brinjal — correctly spelt; the Indian English word for aubergine/eggplant.

NOTE

• Same “-sure” family: measure, treasure, leisure, pleasure, closure, exposure.

• Frequently misspelt SSC words: occurrence, embarrass, maintenance, committee, privilege, separate.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.

Villainous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Nefarious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Villainous = wicked, evil, criminal in nature. (दुष्ट / नीच)

◦ Nefarious also means extremely wicked or criminal, so the two are synonyms.

◦ Correct: The gang was involved in the most nefarious (villainous) activities.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Wholesome = good for health or morally beneficial — an antonym here.

• Lucid = clear, easily understood; also mentally sound.

• Famous = well known, celebrated — not related to wickedness.

NOTE

• Synonyms of villainous/nefarious: heinous, atrocious, diabolical, vile, iniquitous, dastardly.

• Antonyms: virtuous, noble, righteous, upright, benevolent.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

Culpable
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Innocent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Culpable = deserving blame; guilty of wrongdoing. (दोषी / अपराधी)

◦ Innocent = free from guilt or blame, and is therefore its exact opposite.

◦ Correct: The court held him culpable, while his brother was declared innocent.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Rigorous = strict, severe, thorough — unrelated to guilt.

• Reasonable = fair, sensible, moderate.

• Edible = fit to be eaten (opposite: inedible).

NOTE

• Synonyms of culpable: blameworthy, guilty, liable, at fault, censurable.

• Legal term often asked: culpable homicide = causing death with the knowledge that it is likely to cause death.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose ‘No improvement’ as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

The sea wall protected the village in the waves.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. village from.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb “protect” takes the preposition “from” (or “against”) to show the danger guarded against: *protect somebody from something*. (से रक्षा करना)

◦ “In” shows position and cannot express the sense of shielding.

◦ Correct: The sea wall protected the village from the waves.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is wrong because “protected the village in the waves” is unidiomatic.

• Option 3 “village through” wrongly suggests movement across something.

• Option 4 “village by” would indicate the agent/means, not the threat.

NOTE

• Verbs + from: prevent from, prohibit from, prevent, hinder from, refrain from, deter from, save from.

• “Protect against” is also correct: *vaccines protect against disease*.

question:
Select the appropriate synonym for the underlined word.

John says, “I am serious.”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. severe.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Serious = solemn, grave, not joking; earnest in manner. (गंभीर)

◦ Severe likewise carries the sense of grave, stern and serious, so it is the closest synonym among the options.

◦ Correct: John says, “I am serious (severe)” — i.e. he is in a grave, earnest mood.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Safe = free from danger — unrelated in meaning.

• Comical = funny, amusing — an antonym of serious.

• Light = not heavy; also light-hearted or frivolous — again an antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of serious: grave, solemn, earnest, sober, sombre, stern.

• Antonyms of serious: frivolous, jovial, flippant, trivial, light-hearted.

question:
Select the most appropriate word for the given group of words.

A large, tall cupboard in which clothes may be hung or stored
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Wardrobe.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A wardrobe is a large, tall cupboard or closet in which clothes are hung or stored. (अलमारी / कपड़ों की आलमारी)

◦ It can also mean a person’s entire collection of clothes: *her summer wardrobe*.

◦ Correct: She hung her coat in the wardrobe.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Hypergamy = the practice of marrying into a higher social class or caste.

• Gibber = to speak rapidly and unintelligibly, to jabber.

• Honorary = a position or degree held as an honour, without payment or without the usual requirements.

NOTE

• Related storage words: cupboard, closet, almirah, chest of drawers, larder (food store), granary (grain store), arsenal (weapon store).

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: He wondered about lots of things.
option_2: He wondered about lotts of things.
option_3: He wondared about lots of things.
option_4: He wondered about lots of thinggs.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He wondered about lots of things.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Every word in Option 1 is spelt correctly — wondered, lots, things. (सोचना / आश्चर्य करना)

◦ “Wonder about” means to think curiously about something.

◦ Correct: He wondered about lots of things.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 misspells “lots” as “lotts” (double t).

• Option 3 misspells “wondered” as “wondared” (a for e).

• Option 4 misspells “things” as “thinggs” (double g).

NOTE

• Do not confuse wonder (to think/marvel) with wander (to roam aimlessly).

• Similar traps: quiet/quite, lose/loose, desert/dessert, stationary/stationery.

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

I _______ only a few steps before I was forced to stop.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. had walked.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• When two actions happen in the past, the earlier action takes the past perfect (had + V3) and the later one takes the simple past. (पूर्ण भूतकाल)

◦ With the conjunction “before”, the clause preceding it normally carries the past perfect: *had + past participle ... before + simple past*.

◦ Correct: I had walked only a few steps before I was forced to stop.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 “have walked” is present perfect and clashes with the past verb “was forced”.

• Option 3 “walk” is simple present and breaks the tense sequence.

• Option 4 “walked” is possible in loose speech but does not bring out the prior completion that “before” demands here.

NOTE

• Structure: Had + V3 ... before/when + V2 and After + had + V3, ... + V2.

• Example: The train had left before we reached the station.

question:
Select the appropriate antonym for the underlined word.

A mysterious glowing girl has informed him of the death.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. evident.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Mysterious = difficult to understand, explain or identify; secretive. (रहस्यमय)

◦ Evident = clearly seen or understood, obvious — hence the exact opposite.

◦ Correct: The reason was not mysterious at all; it was quite evident to everyone.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Cryptic = having a hidden meaning, puzzling — a synonym, not an antonym.

• Critical = crucial, or fault-finding — unrelated.

• Murky = dark, gloomy, obscure — again close in sense to mysterious.

NOTE

• Synonyms of mysterious: enigmatic, inscrutable, arcane, baffling, obscure.

• Synonyms of evident: apparent, manifest, patent, conspicuous, palpable.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose ‘No improvement’ as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

Dr. Mark said I can came to his office on Friday or Saturday of next week.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. come to his office on.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A modal auxiliary (can, may, will, must, should) is always followed by the bare infinitive (V1), never by V2/V3. (सहायक क्रिया + मूल क्रिया)

◦ So “can came” is wrong; it must be “can come”.

◦ The preposition “on” is correct with days of the week (*on Friday*), so only the verb needs correction.

◦ Correct: Dr. Mark said I can come to his office on Friday or Saturday of next week.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is wrong because “can came” is grammatically incorrect.

• Option 2 “coming to his office at” wrongly uses a participle after “can” and the wrong preposition.

• Option 3 “comes to his office in” adds ‘s’ after a modal and uses “in” with a day.

NOTE

• Prepositions of time: at → clock time (at 5 p.m.); on → days/dates (on Monday, on 15 August); in → months/years/long periods (in May, in 2023).

• Modal + V1: *He must go, She should write, They will come.*

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

“Why?” said Harry in surprise. “There is a (1) ______, Harry Potter. A plot to make most terrible things (2) ______ at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry (3) ______,” whispered Dobby, suddenly trembling all over. “Dobby has (4) ______ months, sir. Harry Potter (5) ______ in peril.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. plot.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Plot = a secret plan to do something harmful or illegal; a conspiracy. (षड़्यंत्र)

◦ The very next sentence of the passage explains the blank: “A plot to make most terrible things happen …”, so the word must be repeated in blank 1.

◦ Correct: There is a plot, Harry Potter.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Paper, notebook and diary are all writing materials and do not fit the idea of a secret, dangerous scheme.

• None of them can be followed by “to make most terrible things happen” in the explanatory sentence.

NOTE

• Cloze tip: when the following sentence repeats a word, that word is almost always the answer.

• Synonyms of plot: conspiracy, scheme, intrigue, machination; as a verb, “plot” = to plan secretly.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

“Why?” said Harry in surprise. “There is a (1) ______, Harry Potter. A plot to make most terrible things (2) ______ at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry (3) ______,” whispered Dobby, suddenly trembling all over. “Dobby has (4) ______ months, sir. Harry Potter (5) ______ in peril.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. happen.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The causative verb “make” is followed by an object + bare infinitive (V1) — *make somebody do something*. (प्रेरणार्थक क्रिया)

◦ Here the object is “most terrible things”, so the verb after it must be the bare form happen, without “to” and without any inflection.

◦ Correct: A plot to make most terrible things happen at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 “happens” wrongly adds ‘s’ after the causative “make”.

• Option 3 “happening” (V-ing) is not used after “make” in this causative pattern.

• Option 4 “happened” (V2/V3) would give a passive-like sense that does not fit.

NOTE

• Bare infinitive after: make, let, bid, see, hear, watch, feel — *I made him write it; She let me go.*

• But in the passive, “make” takes the to-infinitive: *He was made to write it.*

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

“Why?” said Harry in surprise. “There is a (1) ______, Harry Potter. A plot to make most terrible things (2) ______ at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry (3) ______,” whispered Dobby, suddenly trembling all over. “Dobby has (4) ______ months, sir. Harry Potter (5) ______ in peril.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. this year.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Dobby is warning Harry about a danger in the current, ongoing school year, so the near demonstrative “this” is required. (इस वर्ष)

◦ This points to something near in time or place; that/those point to something distant.

◦ Correct: A plot to make most terrible things happen at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry this year.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 “those years” is plural and vague; the plot refers to one specific session.

• Option 2 “that year” wrongly points to a remote past year, whereas the danger is immediate.

• Option 3 “the year” is incomplete without further defining words.

NOTE

• Demonstratives: this (singular, near), these (plural, near), that (singular, far), those (plural, far).

• Time phrases such as this year, this morning, last night, next week take no preposition.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

“Why?” said Harry in surprise. “There is a (1) ______, Harry Potter. A plot to make most terrible things (2) ______ at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry (3) ______,” whispered Dobby, suddenly trembling all over. “Dobby has (4) ______ months, sir. Harry Potter (5) ______ in peril.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. known it for.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence already begins with “Dobby has …”, so the blank needs the past participle (V3) to complete the present perfect tense: *has known*. (पूर्ण वर्तमान काल)

◦ “For” is used with a period of time (“months”), while “since” is used with a point of time.

◦ Correct: Dobby has known it for months, sir.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 “had knowing for” is doubly wrong — “had” after “has”, plus a V-ing form.

• Option 3 “had acknowledging for” has the same structural error.

• Option 4 “been known since” gives a passive sense and wrongly uses “since” with the period “months”.

NOTE

• For + length of time: *for two hours, for months, for a long time*.

• Since + starting point: *since Monday, since 2010, since morning*.

• Stative verbs like know, believe, own are not used in continuous tenses.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

“Why?” said Harry in surprise. “There is a (1) ______, Harry Potter. A plot to make most terrible things (2) ______ at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry (3) ______,” whispered Dobby, suddenly trembling all over. “Dobby has (4) ______ months, sir. Harry Potter (5) ______ in peril.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. must not put himself.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed collocation is “put oneself in peril/danger”, and the modal “must not” expresses a strong prohibition or urgent warning, which suits Dobby’s frightened warning. (खतरे में डालना)

◦ The reflexive pronoun for “Harry Potter” (third person, masculine) is himself, written as one word.

◦ Correct: Harry Potter must not put himself in peril.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 “insert himself” does not collocate with “in peril”.

• Option 2 “his self” is wrong — the reflexive pronoun is one word, “himself”.

• Option 3 “might not put oneself” weakens the warning and uses the wrong pronoun for a named person.

NOTE

• Reflexive pronouns: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves.

• Must not = prohibition; need not = absence of necessity; may not = lack of permission.
